1.title: Configuration and Cluster Administration
1.text: Welcome to Module 4: Configuration and Cluster Administration. This module is in the Kubernetes Fundamentals domain, and it covers the topic called Administration. By the end you will be able to do four things. Use Config Maps and Secrets, and say what protects a Secret. Set requests and limits, and apply Limit Range and Resource Quota. Describe cluster setup, upgrades, version skew and E T C D backup. And take a node out of service safely with cordon, drain and Pod Disruption Budgets.

1.title: Case Check-In: Harbor Books Runs the Shop for Real
1.text: Harbor Books is moving from a trial to the real shop. Settings such as the database host and the payment key must not live in the image. The shop must not starve other teams, and the platform engineer wants a quota for it. One worker node needs patching, and the cluster needs upgrades and backups. In this module you set up configuration, limits and routine maintenance.

1.title: ConfigMaps
1.text: A Config Map stores non-confidential settings as key value pairs, separate from the code. The same image can run in development and in production with different Config Maps. The data field holds text values, and the binary data field holds binary values. A Config Map is limited to one mebibyte, and it gives no secrecy or encryption. The snippet shows a Config Map with a database host and a log level. Exam tip: anything you would be happy to see in a public repository belongs in a Config Map, and anything confidential does not.

1.title: Using a ConfigMap in a Pod
1.text: A Pod can use a Config Map in two ways. As environment variables: env from loads every key, and config map key ref picks one key. Or as files, in a read-only volume mounted into the container. The snippet does both with the same Config Map. The Config Map and the Pod must share a namespace. Exam tip: a Config Map reaches a container as environment variables or as files.

1.title: Secrets: Encoded, Not Encrypted
1.text: A Secret holds confidential values such as passwords, tokens and keys, outside Pod specs and images. Values in a manifest are base sixty-four encoded. That is encoding, not encryption. By default, Secrets are stored unencrypted in E T C D, and anyone with A P I access, or access to E T C D, can read them. So protect them. Enable encryption at rest. Use role-based access control, R B A C, with least privilege. Limit access to specific containers. Or use an external secret store. Exam tip: base sixty-four is not encryption.

1.title: Resource Requests and Limits
1.text: A request is what the container needs. The scheduler uses it to place the Pod, and the kube let reserves it. A limit is the most the container may use, and the kube let enforces it. C P U is measured in C P U units. One is a whole physical core, and five hundred millicpu is half a core. Memory is measured in bytes, with suffixes such as M I. The snippet sets a request and a limit for both. Exam tip: requests are for scheduling, and limits are for enforcement.

1.title: What Requests and Limits Do
1.text: A container may use more than its request if the node has room to spare. Over its C P U limit, a container is throttled. Over its memory limit, the kernel may kill it, when memory is under pressure. So C P U limits slow a container down, while memory limits can stop it. The diagram shows the request on the left, deciding placement, and the limit on the right, enforced at run time. Exam tip: C P U is throttled, and memory is killed.

1.title: LimitRange and ResourceQuota
1.text: Two objects control resources in a namespace. A Limit Range constrains the requests and limits of each Pod or container: a minimum, a maximum, a ratio, and defaults. A Resource Quota limits the total resources used in the whole namespace, and the number of objects of a kind. A cluster administrator creates at least one Resource Quota for each namespace. And a Limit Range can fill in default requests and limits for containers that set none. Exam tip: Limit Range shapes each object, and Resource Quota caps the namespace.

1.title: Cluster Setup with kubeadm
1.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. Kube A D M builds a cluster in a few steps. Kube A D M init initializes the first control plane node. Then you install a Pod network add-on, so that Pods can communicate. Kube A D M join, with a token, adds the other nodes. And when you work with several clusters, keep one kube config context for each, and switch with kube control config use context. Exam tip: init for the control plane, join for the rest.

1.title: Upgrades and Version Skew
1.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. It is also tagged moving, because the skew numbers can change. You upgrade in order: the control plane first, then the worker nodes. You go one minor version at a time, because skipping minor versions is not supported. And you drain a node before a minor version kube let upgrade. As of the thirtieth of October, twenty twenty-six, the kube let can lag the A P I server by up to three minor versions. The controller manager and the scheduler can lag it by one. Exam tip: components may lag the A P I server, but never lead it.

1.title: etcd Backup and Restore
1.text: E T C D holds all cluster data, so back it up. A backup is a snapshot, taken with E T C D C T L snapshot save. A restore uses E T C D U T L snapshot restore. E T C D C T L is the client that talks to E T C D over the network. E T C D U T L works directly on E T C D data files. The snippet saves a snapshot, checks its status, and restores it. Exam tip: save with E T C D C T L, and restore with E T C D U T L.

2.title: Node Maintenance: Cordon, Drain and PodDisruptionBudgets
2.text: Three commands take a node out of service. Cordon marks a node unschedulable, so no new Pods land on it. Drain safely evicts the Pods, respecting Pod Disruption Budgets, and the ignore daemon sets flag skips Daemon Set Pods. Uncordon makes the node schedulable again. A Pod Disruption Budget limits how many Pods of an app may be down at once during voluntary disruptions, such as a drain. Exam tip: drain first, patch second, uncordon last.

2.title: Releases, Deprecation and Support
2.text: This slide is tagged moving. Kubernetes has about three releases a year. Each minor release gets about one year of patch support, plus two months of maintenance, fourteen months in all. For A P I versions, G A versions, the generally available ones, may be deprecated, but they are not removed within a major version. Beta versions are deprecated within nine months or three releases, and are no longer served nine months or three releases after that, whichever is longer. Alpha versions can disappear in any release, without notice. As of the thirtieth of October, twenty twenty-six, version one point thirty-seven is the latest minor release. Exam tip: stable A P I s are not removed within a major version, and alpha ones can vanish at any time.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Configuration and Administration
2.text: Six pairs to keep apart. Config Map or Secret: settings anyone may see, or confidential data. Base sixty-four or encryption: base sixty-four only encodes, and encryption at rest protects Secrets in E T C D. Request or limit: requests place the Pod, and limits are enforced. Limit Range or Resource Quota: per object, or the whole namespace. Cordon or drain: cordon stops new Pods, and drain also evicts the running ones. And upgrade order: the control plane first, one minor version at a time. Exam tip: when a question names a limit, ask who enforces it.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: To recap. Config Maps hold non-confidential settings, as environment variables or files, and Secrets hold confidential data that needs protection beyond base sixty-four. Requests place Pods and limits are enforced. A Limit Range shapes objects, and a Resource Quota caps a namespace. Kube A D M init and join build the cluster, and a Pod network add-on connects it. Upgrade the control plane first, one minor version at a time, and snapshot E T C D. And for maintenance, cordon, drain with Pod Disruption Budgets, then uncordon. Now nine practice questions.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which statement about Config Maps is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A Config Map keeps non-confidential settings separate from the code. It gives no encryption, so it is not meant for passwords. It is limited to one mebibyte, and a Pod can use only Config Maps from its own namespace.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Harbor Books runs the same storefront image in staging and in production, with a different database host in each. What is the best way to supply the host? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A Config Map keeps settings apart from the image, so one image can serve both environments, and the Pod receives the value as an environment variable or a file. Building separate images defeats that, a database host is not confidential, and edits inside a container are lost on restart.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A Secret's value in a manifest is base sixty-four encoded. What does that mean? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Base sixty-four is an encoding, not encryption, so anyone who can read the Secret can decode it. By default, Secrets are also stored unencrypted in E T C D, which is why encryption at rest and tight access rules are recommended.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A Pod requests five hundred millicpu of C P U and two hundred fifty-six M I of memory. What does the scheduler do with these requests? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. The scheduler uses requests to decide which node can fit the Pod, and the kube let reserves that amount for the container. Capping and terminating are enforcement of limits, not requests.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. One container goes over its C P U limit, and another goes over its memory limit. What happens? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. C P U limits are enforced by throttling, and memory limits by out of memory kills when the kernel sees memory pressure. Limits are not raised automatically, and C P U over-use does not terminate a container.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. The platform engineer wants to cap the total C P U and memory that all Pods in the shop namespace can use together. Which object does that? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A Resource Quota limits the total resources used in a namespace. A Limit Range constrains the requests and limits of each object, a Pod Disruption Budget limits voluntary disruption, and a Config Map only holds settings.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Which statement about upgrading a kube A D M cluster is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. The control plane is upgraded first, then the worker nodes, and minor versions cannot be skipped. Components such as the kube let may lag the A P I server, but must not be newer than it.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. How do you take a backup of the data in E T C D? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. E T C D is backed up with a snapshot, taken with E T C D C T L snapshot save, and restored with E T C D U T L snapshot restore. The kube let configuration and kube control output do not hold the cluster's data, and kube A D M upgrade plan only reports available upgrades.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. Harbor Books must patch a worker node without taking the storefront down. Which sequence is right? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Drain cordons the node and evicts its Pods safely, respecting Pod Disruption Budgets, so the app keeps its minimum availability. Uncordon makes the node usable again afterwards. Cordon alone leaves the Pods running on the node.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are the answers at a glance. Question one, B: a Config Map holds non-confidential settings. Question two, A: a Config Map per environment keeps the image the same. Question three, D: base sixty-four is encoding, not encryption. Question four, C: the scheduler places Pods by their requests. Question five, A: C P U is throttled, and memory over-use can kill. Question six, B: a Resource Quota caps a namespace. Question seven, C: control plane first, one minor version at a time. Question eight, D: E T C D C T L snapshot save. Question nine, C: drain, patch, uncordon.
